short_definition: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative you give up when you make a choice, measured in money, time or other benefits you could have had instead.
explanation: Opportunity cost exists because money, time and attention spent on one thing can't be spent on something else. The question it asks is: 'What is the best option I'm giving up?' Opportunity cost never appears on an invoice or an income statement, but it is real. For example, a business owner who spends ten hours on bookkeeping gives up ten hours of selling.

Opportunity cost matters because many decisions look good on their own but worse next to the alternative. Businesses use it to choose between projects. Individuals can use it to compare options such as paying down debt versus investing, or a lower-paid job with more free time versus a higher-paid one.

Opportunity cost is usually an estimate, because you are comparing a known choice with a guess about what might have happened otherwise. Use it as a thinking tool, not a precise number. Non-financial factors such as stress, risk and enjoyment belong in the comparison too.
example: Illustrative example: you have $3,000. You could pay off a credit card charging an illustrative 20% APR, or keep the cash in a savings account paying an illustrative 4%. Keeping the cash earns about $120 in a year, but you go on paying roughly $600 in card interest. The opportunity cost of keeping the cash is about $600 of avoidable interest, which leaves you roughly $480 worse off. This simplified example ignores the need for an emergency buffer, which may matter more.
common_mistake: Counting only the money spent and ignoring what you give up, especially time. Spending a whole weekend to save $30 on a DIY job may not be worth it if those hours could have earned or given you much more.
title: Opportunity Cost
